explanation: The summit is limestone that formed on an ancient seabed, with remains of trilobites and sea lilies. The collision of India with Asia later pushed it up.

claims.text: Limestone near the summit of Mount Everest contains fossils of marine animals.
The fossils near Everest's summit are not of dinosaurs, Ice Age mammals or flying reptiles; the rock is older than any of them.
The rock at Everest's summit is limestone formed on an ancient seabed.
Fossils near Everest's summit include trilobites and crinoids, also called sea lilies.
The collision of the Indian plate with Asia raised the rocks of the Himalayas.

evidence.restatement: The limestone near Everest's summit holds fossils of marine animals.
The summit limestone is Ordovician, about 450 to 470 million years old, older than any dinosaur, pterosaur or Ice Age mammal.
The summit rock is limestone laid down on an ancient sea floor.
Trilobites and crinoids (sea lilies) are among the fossils found there.
India's collision with Asia raised the Himalaya.
The summit limestone of Everest (Qomolangma Formation, Ordovician) contains marine fossils such as crinoids and trilobites.
That limestone is about 450 million years old, older than dinosaurs, pterosaurs and Ice Age mammals.
Everest's summit pyramid is limestone laid down on an ancient seabed.
Fossils in the Qomolangma Formation include trilobites and crinoids (sea lilies).
The Himalayas rose from the collision of the Indian plate with Asia.
